name: Ur Urban Plan
sacred_precinct: ["Ziggurat of Ur-Nammu","Temple of Nanna","Giparu priestess residence"]
description: Third Dynasty of Ur capital with sacred temenos dominating the city center, dense residential quarters of courtyard houses accessed by narrow winding alleys, and a harbor district for river trade
sources: ["Woolley 1934 Excavations at Ur","Crawford 2015 Ur: The City of the Moon God"]

name: Uruk City Plan
description: Oldest major city with two distinct sacred precincts (Eanna for Inanna, Anu ziggurat), massive defensive walls attributed to Gilgamesh, and extensive urban area making it the largest settlement of 4th millennium BCE
sources: ["Nissen 2001 Uruk: Early Cities","Finkbeiner 1991 Uruk Kampagne"]

name: Babylon Grid
description: Neo-Babylonian capital bisected by the Euphrates with monumental Processional Way leading through the Ishtar Gate, massive double-wall fortifications, and the sacred Esagila district containing the great ziggurat Etemenanki
sources: ["Koldewey 1914 The Excavations at Babylon","Pedersen 2005 Archive und Bibliotheken in Babylon"]

name: Nineveh Royal Plan
districts: ["Kuyunjik palace mound","Nebi Yunus arsenal","residential quarters","garden district"]
description: Assyrian capital dominated by two great mounds—Kuyunjik with Sennacherib's Palace Without Rival and its famous garden terraces, and Nebi Yunus arsenal—enclosed by 12 km of fortification walls with 15 monumental gates
sources: ["Russell 1991 Sennacherib's Palace Without Rival","Reade 2000 Ninive (Nineveh)"]

name: Mohenjo-daro Grid
districts: ["citadel (upper town)","lower town residential","granary complex","Great Bath precinct"]
water_management: ["sophisticated brick-lined drains","covered sewers","wells in every block"]
description: Remarkably planned Indus Valley city with strict orthogonal grid, sophisticated drainage and sanitation rivaling modern cities, raised citadel with Great Bath, and standardized brick construction throughout
sources: ["Marshall 1931 Mohenjo-daro","Kenoyer 1998 Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley"]

name: Harappa City Plan
districts: ["Mound AB citadel","Mound E lower town","Mound F cemetery","granary area"]
description: Twin city to Mohenjo-daro with similar orthogonal planning, extensive craft production areas including bead-making workshops, and standardized architecture reflecting centralized urban planning authority
sources: ["Vats 1940 Excavations at Harappa","Meadow 1991 Harappa Excavations"]

name: Athens Classical Plan
description: Classical Athens with Acropolis as sacred crown, Agora as civic heart with stoas and public buildings, Pnyx for democratic assembly, connected to port of Piraeus by Long Walls creating a fortified corridor
sources: ["Camp 2001 The Archaeology of Athens","Travlos 1971 Pictorial Dictionary of Ancient Athens"]

name: Miletus Hippodamian Grid
description: Birthplace of the Hippodamian grid plan, rebuilt after Persian destruction with rational orthogonal layout, separate civic and commercial agoras, and regular residential blocks—the prototype for planned Greek and Roman cities
sources: ["Von Gerkan 1924 Griechische Stadteanlagen","Burns 1976 Hippodamus and the Planned City"]

name: Rome Imperial Plan
residential_zones: ["insulae apartments (up to 7 stories)","Subura dense quarter","domus elite houses"]
description: Imperial Rome grew organically over seven hills to house over a million inhabitants, with monumental public architecture (fora, baths, amphitheaters), sophisticated infrastructure (aqueducts, sewers), and dense residential insulae up to seven stories
sources: ["Stambaugh 1988 The Ancient Roman City","Claridge 2010 Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide"]

name: Pompeii Plan
sacred_precinct: ["Temple of Jupiter","Temple of Apollo","Temple of Isis"]
description: Preserved Roman city revealing everyday urban life: mixed commercial-residential streets, forum as civic center, sophisticated water distribution from castellum aquae, and diverse housing from elite domus to modest upper-floor apartments
sources: ["Zanker 1998 Pompeii: Public and Private Life","Wallace-Hadrill 1994 Houses and Society in Pompeii"]

name: Chang'an Tang Grid
districts: ["imperial palace (Daming)","administrative city","108 walled wards","East Market","West Market"]
fortifications: ["rammed-earth outer wall (36 km)","ward walls with gates"]
description: Tang Dynasty capital and world's largest city of its era, with strict grid of 108 walled wards bisected by the grand Zhuque Avenue, massive enclosed markets, and imperial palace complex at the northern terminus of the central axis
sources: ["Xiong 2000 Sui-Tang Chang'an","Heng 1999 Cities of Aristocrats and Bureaucrats"]

name: Beijing Imperial Grid
fortifications: ["Inner City wall","Outer City wall","Forbidden City wall and moat"]
public_spaces: ["Tiananmen Square area","Temple of Heaven park","imperial gardens"]
sacred_precinct: ["Temple of Heaven","Temple of Earth","Forbidden City temples","Confucius Temple"]
description: Ming-Qing capital organized along a powerful central axis running through the nested enclosures of Forbidden City, Imperial City, and Inner City, with hutong neighborhoods of courtyard houses and cardinal-direction temple complexes
sources: ["Steinhardt 1990 Chinese Imperial City Planning","Naquin 2000 Peking: Temples and City Life"]

name: Kyoto Imperial Grid
description: Heian-kyo modeled on Tang Chang'an but adapted to Japanese topography, with a grid of numbered avenues, the Imperial Palace at north center, and distinctive machiya townhouses—notably lacking city walls unlike its Chinese model
sources: ["Fiévé 2008 Atlas historique de Kyōto","Stavros 2014 Kyoto: An Urban History"]

name: Tenochtitlan Plan
major_axes: ["four great causeways to cardinal points","central temple axis"]
water_management: ["chinampas (floating gardens)","aqueducts from Chapultepec","dikes for flood control"]
fortifications: ["lake as natural defense","causeways with removable bridges"]
description: Island capital of the Aztec Empire built on Lake Texcoco, divided into four quarters by causeways aligned to cardinal directions, with the Sacred Precinct at center, extensive chinampa agriculture, and sophisticated hydraulic engineering including aqueducts, dikes, and flood control
sources: ["Smith 2012 The Aztecs","Calnek 1976 The Internal Structure of Tenochtitlan"]

name: Cusco Puma Plan
description: Inca capital designed in the shape of a puma with Sacsayhuaman as the head and Coricancha as the tail, divided into upper (Hanan) and lower (Hurin) moieties, serving as the axis mundi from which four roads led to the four quarters (suyus) of the empire
sources: ["Hyslop 1990 Inka Settlement Planning","Bauer 2004 Ancient Cuzco"]

name: Great Zimbabwe Plan
description: Southern African stone city with three distinct zones—the Hill Complex for elite/ritual activity, the Great Enclosure with its iconic conical tower and massive free-standing stone walls, and the Valley Enclosures for general habitation and craft production
sources: ["Pikirayi 2001 The Zimbabwe Culture","Huffman 2007 Handbook to the Iron Age"]

name: Angkor Thom Plan
fortifications: ["laterite wall (3 km per side)","5 monumental gates","100m moat"]
public_spaces: ["Bayon temple terrace","Royal Palace plaza","Terrace of Elephants"]
description: Khmer capital designed as a microcosm of the Hindu-Buddhist universe with the Bayon temple at the exact center representing Mount Meru, enclosed by walls and moat representing the cosmic ocean and mountain ranges, with monumental causeways and gate towers
sources: ["Coe 2003 Angkor and the Khmer Civilization","Jacques 1997 Angkor"]

name: Benin City Plan
districts: ["Oba's Palace (center)","inner ward chiefs' quarters","outer residential wards","earthwork perimeter"]
fortifications: ["massive earthworks (16,000 km total network)","inner and outer walls","moats"]
description: Edo/Benin capital with massive earthwork fortifications among the largest pre-mechanical constructions in the world, organized concentrically around the Oba's palace, with specialized guild quarters and a sophisticated system of wards governed by chiefs
sources: ["Connah 1975 The Archaeology of Benin","Osadolor 2001 The Military System of Benin Kingdom"]

name: Timgad Roman Colony
sacred_precinct: ["Capitoline Temple","Temple of the Genius of the Colony"]
description: Textbook example of Roman colonial grid planning founded by Trajan for veterans, with perfect orthogonal street grid, central forum at cardo-decumanus intersection, and uniform residential blocks—later outgrew its walls with organic suburban expansion
sources: ["Ballu 1911 Les ruines de Timgad","Lassus 1981 La forteresse byzantine de Thamugadi"]

name: Tikal Plan
districts: ["Great Plaza","North Acropolis","Central Acropolis","Lost World complex","residential periphery"]
fortifications: ["massive earthwork and ditch system","temple height as defense"]
description: Major Maya city with dispersed settlement pattern—monumental ceremonial centers connected by sacbe causeways surrounded by low-density residential compounds, innovative water management in seasonal wetlands, and towering temple-pyramids as cosmological markers
sources: ["Harrison 1999 The Lords of Tikal","Martin 2000 Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens"]

name: Djenne-Djenno Plan
residential_zones: ["mudbrick round and rectangular houses on tells"]
description: One of sub-Saharan Africa's oldest cities, organized as a cluster of specialized tells around a central mound rather than a single walled settlement, demonstrating an indigenous African model of urbanism without centralized defensive architecture
sources: ["McIntosh 1995 Excavations at Jenne-Jeno","McIntosh 2005 Ancient Middle Niger"]

name: Constantinople Plan
districts: ["Great Palace complex","Hippodrome","Hagia Sophia district","commercial quarters","Blachernae palace"]
fortifications: ["Theodosian Walls (triple land wall)","sea walls","Golden Horn chain"]
sacred_precinct: ["Hagia Sophia","Church of Holy Apostles","numerous churches and monasteries"]
description: Byzantine capital on a strategic peninsula defended by the legendary Theodosian triple walls, with the Mese boulevard connecting multiple imperial fora, the Hippodrome for public spectacle, and Hagia Sophia as the spiritual center of Eastern Christendom
sources: ["Mango 2000 Le développement urbain de Constantinople","Freely 2000 Istanbul: The Imperial City"]

name: Cahokia Plan
major_axes: ["central north-south axis through Monks Mound","east-west equinox alignment"]
description: Largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico centered on Monks Mound (the largest earthwork in the Americas), with a vast Grand Plaza, astronomical Woodhenge circle, and planned central axis reflecting a cosmological vision unique to Mississippian culture
sources: ["Pauketat 2009 Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City","Young 1975 Cahokia: The Great Native American Metropolis"]

name: Jericho Tell Plan
description: Among the world's earliest permanent settlements with the oldest known stone fortification wall and tower, demonstrating the transition from round to rectangular house plans and early communal ritual in the form of plastered ancestor skulls
sources: ["Kenyon 1957 Digging Up Jericho","Bar-Yosef 1986 The Walls of Jericho"]

name: Catalhoyuk Plan
districts: ["densely packed houses (single zone)","midden areas","possible ritual buildings"]
fortifications: ["outer house walls as perimeter (no formal fortification)"]
residential_zones: ["identical contiguous mudbrick houses","roof entry via ladders"]
description: Neolithic proto-city with no streets—houses built wall-to-wall with rooftop access via ladders, extensive intramural burial beneath house floors, and elaborately painted interior shrines with bull imagery, representing a radically egalitarian settlement model
sources: ["Hodder 2006 The Leopard's Tale","Mellaart 1967 Catal Huyuk"]

name: Teotihuacan Grid
major_axes: ["Avenue of the Dead (N-S, 15.5° east of north)","east-west axis"]
districts: ["Pyramid of the Sun","Pyramid of the Moon","Ciudadela","apartment compounds"]
public_spaces: ["Moon Plaza","Ciudadela courtyard","Avenue of the Dead plazas"]
residential_zones: ["standardized multi-family apartment compounds","up to 100 residents each"]
sacred_precinct: ["Pyramid of the Sun","Pyramid of the Moon","Temple of the Feathered Serpent"]
description: Mesoamerica's first true metropolis with a grid aligned to a specific astronomical orientation, the monumental Avenue of the Dead, and unique standardized multi-family apartment compounds housing the entire urban population—unlike any other ancient American city
sources: ["Millon 1973 Urbanization at Teotihuacan","Cowgill 2015 Ancient Teotihuacan"]

name: Machu Picchu Plan
fortifications: ["steep terrain as natural defense","single controlled entry"]
public_spaces: ["Sacred Plaza","Intihuatana platform","Temple of the Three Windows"]
sacred_precinct: ["Intihuatana stone","Temple of the Sun","Room of Three Windows"]
description: Royal Inca estate dramatically sited on a mountain ridge with integration of architecture and landscape, sophisticated water engineering feeding 16 ceremonial fountains, and precise stone masonry aligned to astronomical events
sources: ["Bingham 1930 Machu Picchu: A Citadel of the Incas","Wright 2006 Machu Picchu: A Civil Engineering Marvel"]

name: Fatehpur Sikri Plan
districts: ["Jami Masjid precinct","palace complex","harem quarters","administrative courts","bazaar street"]
description: Mughal Emperor Akbar's planned capital blending Hindu, Islamic, and Jain architectural elements, organized around a series of progressive courtyards from public to private, abandoned after only 14 years possibly due to water scarcity
sources: ["Brand 1993 Fatehpur Sikri","Rizvi 1972 Fatehpur Sikri"]

name: Timbuktu Plan
districts: ["Djinguereber mosque quarter","Sankore mosque/university quarter","Sidi Yahia quarter","market areas"]
description: Trans-Saharan trade city and center of Islamic scholarship, organized around three great mosques that also served as universities, with banco architecture adapted to desert climate and a cosmopolitan population of scholars, traders, and artisans
sources: ["Insoll 2003 The Archaeology of Islam in Sub-Saharan Africa","Hunwick 1999 Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire"]

name: Persepolis Terrace Plan
fortifications: ["massive stone terrace platform (125,000 m²)","mudbrick fortification wall"]
public_spaces: ["Apadana courtyard","Gate of All Nations","grand staircase platform"]
description: Achaemenid ceremonial capital built on a massive stone platform, designed as a stage for royal audiences and tribute reception, with the grand Apadana hall and its famous staircase reliefs depicting the empire's diverse subject peoples
sources: ["Schmidt 1953 Persepolis I","Curtis 2005 Forgotten Empire: Persepolis"]
